Abstract
College events are often announced through notices, messages and separate registration
forms. This arrangement makes it difficult for students to identify relevant activities and for
organizers to maintain a consistent record of available seats, participant details and fee
status. The College Event Management Website, implemented as Campus Commons, brings
these activities into a common platform for students, clubs and administrators.
Students can create an account, maintain a profile, browse clubs and events, join clubs,
register for activities and review their registrations. Clubs maintain organizational profiles
and create events with explicit schedules, venues, fees, capacities and eligibility conditions.
Administrative approval controls which clubs can publish, while moderation tools support
event cancellation and removal from public discovery. Each role receives an interface suited
to its responsibilities.
The frontend uses React, TypeScript, Vite and Tailwind CSS. A Java Spring Boot backend
exposes JSON APIs, applies Spring Security access controls and persists records through
Spring Data JPA. PostgreSQL is the authoritative database, with Flyway migrations defining
a reproducible schema. Supabase PostgreSQL is a compatible hosting option. Session
authentication, CSRF protection, server-side validation and ownership checks protect
state-changing operations. Event-row locks and unique registration constraints prevent
duplicate bookings and oversubscription under concurrent requests.
Free events are confirmed immediately. Paid events reserve a seat for a limited checkout
interval and record payment attempts separately. The implemented payment provider is a
development simulator supporting success, failure, retry and refund scenarios; live financial
settlement is outside the verified implementation. This distinction allows the registration
lifecycle to be evaluated without representing simulated transactions as real payments.
Verification recorded 23 backend integration tests on both H2 and PostgreSQL, 16 frontend
tests and eight full-stack browser workflows. The resulting system demonstrates an
integrated approach to campus event administration, supported by responsive interfaces
and explicit transaction rules. Future work includes a live payment gateway, institutional
identity verification, production deployment and broader accessibility evaluation.
Keywords: college event management, club administration, React, Spring Boot, PostgreSQL, role-based
access, concurrent registration.

1. Introduction
A college event involves more than publishing a title and date. The organizer must
communicate eligibility, reserve a venue, control participation and account for registration
fees. Students need an accurate description of the activity and a reliable indication that their
booking has been accepted. The proposed website connects these responsibilities through
a shared record of clubs, events and registrations.
1.1 Background
Campus activities include technical workshops, cultural programmes, sports meetings and
student-club sessions. Their administration commonly involves a mixture of
announcements, forms and spreadsheets. When the same event is represented in several
places, a revised deadline or venue may not reach every participant. A centralized website
can make the published event record the reference point for students and organizers.
The project uses a browser interface backed by a transactional service. Public information
remains easy to discover, while personal registrations and organizer controls require
authentication. The database stores durable records so that a page refresh or browser
change does not remove a student's booking history.
1.2 Motivation
The primary motivation is to reduce manual coordination while preserving clear
accountability. Students should be able to distinguish an available event from a full or
closed event before attempting registration. Clubs should be able to publish complete
information and review participants without maintaining duplicate lists. Administrators need
a way to review organizations and respond to inappropriate or cancelled events.
A second motivation is technical: registration combines user experience with database
consistency. Two students may request the last available seat at the same time. Correct
behaviour requires server-side rules and transaction boundaries in addition to a
well-designed form.
1.3 Project Scope
The scope covers one college, three user roles, club membership, event publication,
registration and a simulated fee-payment lifecycle. Event eligibility is evaluated against the
department and study year entered in a student profile. Clubs manage their own records,
and administrators review clubs and moderate events. Attendance scanning, certificates,
live payment settlement, verified college identity, email reminders and multi-campus
administration are reserved for later development.

1.4 Technologies Used
React and TypeScript implement reusable pages, typed API models and interactive forms.
Vite provides the development server and production build, while Tailwind CSS supports
responsive styling. React Router organizes navigation; TanStack Query coordinates
requests and refreshed data. [1-4]
Java 21 and Spring Boot provide the backend runtime. Spring Security handles
authentication and request authorization. Spring Data JPA maps application records to
PostgreSQL; Flyway applies schema changes. A session cookie identifies the authenticated
browser. PostgreSQL may run locally or through a compatible managed provider such as
Supabase. [5-9]
2. Problem Statement
The problem is to provide a consistent event-management process in which published
information, registration eligibility, remaining capacity and payment status agree across all
user interfaces. The system must prevent unauthorized edits, duplicate registrations and
acceptance of bookings after an event becomes unavailable.
2.1 Limitations of Existing Systems
A workflow based on separate notices, forms and payment references requires organizers
to reconcile records manually. Capacity may be checked only after submissions arrive, and
students may be uncertain whether submitting a form confirms a seat. General-purpose
tools can support these tasks, but college-specific approval and eligibility rules require
additional coordination.
2.2 Need for an Integrated Event and Club Platform
A shared platform connects an approved club to its published activities and links each
student to a single registration record per event. Schedule, fee and venue changes become
visible through the same event page. Organizers receive participant records from the
booking system, reducing the need to copy data between unrelated tools.
2.3 Importance of Data Privacy and User Experience
Student names, contact details, college identifiers and booking histories should be
disclosed only to authorized users. Authentication alone is insufficient: the backend must
also verify event ownership and registration ownership. The interface must explain
validation errors, payment holds and cancellation outcomes in language that students can
act upon. Labels, visible focus and readable status text support this requirement.

3
2.4 Lack of Personalization and Adaptability
A single undifferentiated event list can obscure relevant opportunities. The website provides
category, date and fee filters, club membership and a student dashboard of upcoming
commitments. Department and year rules tailor eligibility. These are explicit preferences
and business rules; the current system does not infer interests through machine learning.
2.5 Integration and Scalability Issues
Payment services and campus identity systems introduce external dependencies. The
project isolates payment behaviour behind a provider interface and keeps credentials on the
server. Pagination, indexed discovery fields and batched reads limit avoidable database
work. A single Java instance currently stores sessions in memory; multiple instances would
require shared session storage and additional operational testing.

3. Literature Review
This review examines event-administration workflows using primary technical
documentation. The comparison is conceptual; it does not rank commercial products or
claim measured participation outcomes.
3.1 Evolution of Digital Event Management Systems
Online forms simplify collection but do not inherently enforce capacity or publication
authority. Component-based interfaces and transactional APIs connect discovery, booking
and management to shared records. React supplies the interface component model. [1]
3.2 Adaptive and Personalized Event Management Models
Selected categories, joined clubs and upcoming registrations provide transparent
personalization. The project uses these explicit rules. Recommendation models would
require participation data and evaluation before supplementing the current filters.
3.3 Data Visualization and Insight Generation Systems
Event cards summarize schedule, venue, fee and availability. Workspaces place status and
participant counts near relevant actions, reducing interpretation of raw records. Historical
trends and attendance analytics remain future work.
3.4 Integration of Security Features in Digital Applications
Access control is applied to each request and to the record being changed. Spring Security
documents session management, while PostgreSQL and Spring Data JPA provide explicit
locking mechanisms used to coordinate seat allocation. These mechanisms address
different concerns: identity establishes who is acting; transaction control protects shared
capacity. [6-8]

3.6 Research Gaps
The design problem is the gap between collecting registrations and maintaining a
dependable end-to-end process. The following needs remain when notices, registration
forms and payment references are administered independently:
• A single, current record of event schedule, eligibility and availability.
• A consistent link between club approval, publication and booking access.
• Concurrency control when demand reaches the remaining capacity.
• Restricted access to personal records and clear, recoverable error states.
These gaps justify the project's design objectives. They are requirements identified through
workflow analysis, not findings from a formal user study. The verification therefore
assesses functional behaviour and consistency rather than claiming adoption or
satisfaction outcomes.

4. Proposed Model
The proposed model is a three-tier web application with public discovery and authenticated
workspaces. A React single-page application communicates with a Java service through
same-origin JSON APIs. PostgreSQL holds the authoritative domain records. The design
keeps user interaction separate from authorization, validation and transaction processing.
4.1 System Overview
Students, clubs and administrators share the same catalog but receive different controls. A
new club begins in PENDING status and requires approval before publication. Published
events accept registrations only within their booking window and while capacity remains.
Students can inspect their own records, while clubs can inspect registrations for events they
own.

1. Frontend Layer
Pages implement role-specific workflows. Reusable components provide labelled controls, dialogs,
loading states and pagination. The API helper attaches the session credentials and CSRF token to relevant
requests; typed models define the response shape.
2. Backend Layer
Controllers accept validated request DTOs. Services enforce approval, ownership, registration and
cancellation rules. Repositories support persisted queries and row locks. Flyway migrations are
append-only, and Hibernate validates the resulting schema rather than generating it at startup.
3. Security & Integration
Spring Security governs session access and CSRF protection. The backend stores no browser-supplied
authority over roles or fees. Provider configuration and administrator provisioning remain server-side; the
production profile prevents activation of demo accounts or simulated payments.

Figure 4. Entity-relationship model
The model contains seven tables. A user may own at most one club, while a club may organize many
events. Memberships connect students to clubs; registrations connect students to events. A registration
may have several payment-attempt records. Reset tokens belong to a user and are stored as hashes.
Unique student-club and student-event pairs prevent duplicate relationships. A cancelled or expired
registration may be reused for a later attempt, preserving its payment history. Monetary values use integer
paise, and schedule fields use time-zone-aware timestamps. These choices avoid floating-point fee errors
and ambiguous event times.

4.7 Key Features of the Proposed Model
• Unified platform integration: discovery, club membership, bookings and administration
use connected records and a common identity model.
• Responsive updates: successful mutations refresh relevant queries; loading, empty and
failure states remain visible instead of implying completion.
• Interactive interface: filters, event previews and confirmation dialogs support focused
tasks on desktop, tablet and phone layouts.
• Clear data presentation: event cards expose schedule, fee and availability; workspaces
retain registration and payment history.
• Secure data handling: session authentication, CSRF protection and record-level ownership
checks guard sensitive operations.
• Personalization and adaptability: memberships, commitments and explicit filters help
students locate suitable activities.
• Registration integrity: database constraints, server-owned prices and event locks enforce
the core booking rules.

5.2 User Interaction and Data Collection
Information is collected through labelled forms and explicit actions. Students enter account
and profile details, clubs enter event and organization details, and administrators submit
review decisions. Each field is validated for its purpose before the backend persists a
change.
Types of Data Collected
Account data: name, email and credentials. Student data: college identifier, department, year and
interests. Club data: name, category, description and contact details. Event data: schedule, venue,
capacity, fee and eligibility. Transaction data: registration status, timestamps, amount and payment
attempts.
Data Collection Characteristics
Structured input supports repeatable validation. The frontend reports missing fields and obvious format
errors promptly; the backend repeats validation and rejects unknown fields. Different roles supply
different records. Sensitive fields are excluded from public views, and HTTPS is required for a deployed
installation.

5.4 Data Handling & Storage Strategy
PostgreSQL stores authoritative records; the browser caches display data. Transactions
preserve related changes, while unique and foreign keys enforce consistency. A cached
response cannot confirm a seat or payment.
Table 6. Data storage strategy
Storage Type Purpose

reset-token hashes
Server session storage Authenticated session state; currently held by one Java instance
Browser query cache Temporary display data; refreshed after relevant changes
API integration Validated access to domain records through role-restricted DTOs
Protected secret storage BCrypt password hashes and SHA-256 reset-token hashes; deployment

Local Storage Handling
Booking records are not persisted in browser localStorage. Authoritative operations require the backend;
cached interface data cannot authorize transactions or support offline registration.

15
Encrypted Data Storage
Passwords are hashed with BCrypt rather than reversibly encrypted. Reset tokens are stored as SHA-256
hashes and expire after 30 minutes. Database and backup encryption depend on the selected production
infrastructure and were not independently verified in the local deployment. Session cookies use HttpOnly
and SameSite settings, with Secure enabled for production.
API-Based Data Handling
Controllers accept validated DTOs and return consistent JSON errors: 400 for invalid input, 401 for
missing authentication, 403 for forbidden access, 404 for missing records, 409 for conflicting business
state and 429 for rate limiting. Student and club queries are scoped to the authenticated identity. Changes
are committed before the interface is told they succeeded.
Key Characteristics of Data Handling
Indexed queries and bounded pages support retrieval. Batched related-record reads avoid repetitive
lookups. All seat-changing operations lock the event first. Prices are copied from the event, times are
stored as UTC instants and cancellation retains history. A future managed database must use suitable
credentials, transport protection and tested backups.

6. Conclusion
The College Event Management Website implements a connected process for event
discovery, club administration and student registration. Its React interface presents the
same records managed by a Spring Boot backend and PostgreSQL database. Approval
checks govern publication, and ownership rules restrict sensitive operations to the
responsible user or role.
The most significant engineering result is a registration lifecycle that combines availability
checks, expiring holds, payment history and cancellation with database-level consistency.
Local tests confirmed the intended functional boundaries, including simultaneous requests
for the last seat. The system is suitable for academic demonstration; live financial
settlement and production infrastructure remain explicit deployment work.
7. Key Outcomes
1. Successful Integration of Multiple Functionalities
Student discovery, club membership, event publication, registration and administrative review operate
within one application. Related records remain linked instead of being maintained in independent lists.
2. Real-Time Data Processing and Visualization
Committed changes are reflected through refreshed API queries. Event availability and registration states
are presented directly; the implementation does not claim continuous push updates or predictive
analytics.
3. Enhanced User Experience and Interface Design
Responsive pages, labelled forms, clear filters and confirmation dialogs support the main tasks. Phone,
tablet and desktop layouts were checked during browser verification.
4. Effective Implementation of Operational Safety Features
Capacity locks, approval gates and controlled cancellation reduce the risk of conflicting bookings and
unauthorized publication. Development refunds are recorded with the registration history.
5. Secure Data Handling and Privacy Protection
Password hashing, expiring reset tokens, CSRF protection and ownership checks protect account and
registration operations. Public responses exclude sensitive account fields.
6. Efficient Frontend and Backend Architecture
Route-level loading, shared components, pagination and batched data access support maintainability and
responsive interaction. The backend retains authority over business decisions.
7. Modular and Scalable System Design
Separate services, repositories and a payment-provider interface define clear extension points. Horizontal
scaling still requires shared session storage and operational validation.
8. Practical and Real-World Applicability
The verified workflows cover common college-event tasks. Institutional identity, production payments and
deployment controls must be completed before operational rollout.

20
8. Future Enhancements
Future development should preserve the verified booking rules while adding services that
depend on institutional and production infrastructure. The following enhancements extend
the present system without representing them as completed functionality.
1. Progressive Web App (PWA) Implementation
An installable application could cache public event information and support opt-in
reminders. Offline views must clearly indicate when information was last refreshed.
Registration and payment would still require an online server check because cached
capacity cannot guarantee an available seat.
2. Advanced Data Visualization
Organizers could examine registration trends, category participation, cancellations and
event attendance. Such analysis would require defined metrics and an attendance-recording
process. Aggregated reports should minimize unnecessary exposure of student identities.
3. AI-Based Insights and Predictions
A future recommendation component could suggest activities using explicit interests and
participation history. It should be evaluated against a simple filter-based baseline and
provide understandable reasons for recommendations. Demand forecasts would need
sufficient historical data; none are claimed in the present implementation.
4. Enhanced Personalization Features
Students could select preferred notification channels, save filter combinations and
customize dashboard sections. Calendar export and subscription feeds could help
coordinate participation with academic schedules. Preferences should remain editable and
should not change eligibility rules without an explicit organizer policy.
5. Improved Accessibility Features
Further evaluation should include keyboard-only tasks, screen readers, zoom, reflow and
error recovery with representative users. Existing labels and focus indicators provide a
foundation, but automated checks alone cannot establish usability for every assistive
technology. WCAG 2.1 supplies relevant testable criteria. [10]
6. Production Integration and Deployment
A live payment adapter requires verified callbacks, reconciliation and refund handling. Other priorities are
institutional identity verification, external email delivery, tested database backups, HTTPS hosting and
shared session storage before horizontal scaling. Managed PostgreSQL connection settings must be
validated in the selected environment.
